stem: A critical service runs on six identical load-balanced servers with the same operating system, same version and same configuration. A single vendor advisory takes all six offline simultaneously. Which design principle was missing?

options.text: Platform diversity, so a flaw common to one platform cannot affect every node at once
options.why: Redundancy protects against one instance failing independently. Six identical nodes share every flaw, so a common vulnerability is a single point of failure wearing a disguise.

options.text: More redundancy: a seventh identical server
options.why: A seventh copy of the same thing fails for the same reason at the same moment.

options.text: Geographic dispersion across two sites
options.why: That protects against a site-level event. A software flaw travels to the second site unchanged.

options.text: A warm recovery site
options.why: A recovery site is for restoring after a disaster. It does not stop a fleet-wide flaw, and a warm site built identically inherits it.

stem: An organisation moves to a multi-cloud design across two providers. Which risk does this address, and which does it not?

options.text: It addresses a single provider's outage or regional failure; it does not address the organisation's own misconfiguration, which can be replicated to both
options.why: Provider independence is the benefit. Your own identity and configuration mistakes travel with you, and most cloud incidents are customer misconfigurations.

options.text: It addresses misconfiguration risk, because two providers validate each other
options.why: Providers do not review your configuration. Nothing cross-checks the two deployments unless you build it.

options.text: It addresses all availability risk, removing the need for backups
options.why: Availability design does not replace backups. Deleted or corrupted data replicates to both providers promptly.

options.text: It addresses nothing, since both providers run the same hardware
options.why: Independent control planes, operations teams and failure domains are the point, whatever the hardware underneath.

stem: A disaster recovery plan is tested successfully. During a real incident six months later it stalls because the only engineer who knows the failover procedure is on leave and unreachable. Which aspect of capacity planning failed?

options.text: People: there was no trained cover for a role the plan depended on
options.why: Capacity planning covers people as well as kit. A plan with a single point of human failure has not been planned for capacity, however well the technology performs.

options.text: Technology: the failover systems were insufficient
options.why: The stem says the test succeeded, so the technology was adequate.

options.text: Infrastructure: power and cooling at the recovery site
options.why: Nothing indicates a facility constraint.

options.text: The plan should have been tested more frequently
options.why: More testing with the same single engineer reproduces the same dependency.

stem: A secondary site holds enough servers to carry full production load, but its electrical supply and cooling are sized for 40% of it. What has been overlooked?

options.text: Infrastructure capacity: power, cooling and space must carry the load the technology is sized for
options.why: Servers that cannot be powered or cooled are inventory. Infrastructure is named separately precisely because it is assessed separately and often forgotten.

options.text: Technology capacity
options.why: The compute is correctly sized. The constraint sits beneath it.

options.text: People capacity
options.why: No staffing constraint is described.

options.text: The site should be reclassified as cold rather than warm
options.why: Site classification describes readiness of equipment and data, not whether the facility can power what is installed.

stem: A business states it can tolerate losing at most one hour of transactions. Backups currently run nightly at 23:00. What must change, and which metric is being expressed?

options.text: Backup frequency must increase to hourly or continuous; the stated tolerance is the recovery point objective
options.why: RPO is how much data loss is acceptable, and backup frequency is what sets it. A nightly schedule can lose up to twenty-four hours.

options.text: Recovery speed must improve; the tolerance is the recovery time objective
options.why: RTO is how long until service returns. The stem talks about lost transactions, which is data, so it is RPO.

options.text: Retention must be extended so older copies are available
options.why: Retention is how far back you can go. It does not reduce the gap since the last copy.

options.text: Backups must be encrypted to protect the lost transactions
options.why: Encryption addresses disclosure. The requirement here is about how much work disappears.

stem: Offsite backup media are transported by a third-party courier to a storage facility. Which control most directly limits the impact if a cartridge is lost in transit?

options.text: Encrypting the backup media, with keys held separately from the media
options.why: Once media leaves your control, encryption is the remaining control. Keys travelling with the cartridge would defeat it, which is why separation is part of the answer.

options.text: Increasing backup frequency
options.why: That reduces potential data loss and does nothing about a copy in someone else's hands.

options.text: Using a courier with better insurance
options.why: Insurance transfers financial loss. It does not prevent disclosure or a notification obligation.

options.text: Keeping an additional onsite copy
options.why: Helps availability, and the lost cartridge remains readable by whoever has it.

stem: A team has run nightly backups for two years and has never performed a restore. What is the correct characterisation of their position?

options.text: They have an untested hypothesis: until a restore succeeds, there is no evidence the backups are usable or that recovery fits the RTO
options.why: Backup jobs reporting success routinely produce unreadable or incomplete sets. Recovery testing is the only thing that converts a backup into a control.

options.text: They are adequately protected, since the jobs report success
options.why: A successful job means the software finished. It does not mean the output can be restored.

options.text: They need snapshots in addition, which do not require testing
options.why: Snapshots need testing too, and typically share storage with production, so they do not survive what takes the array or the site.

options.text: They should increase retention before testing anything
options.why: Keeping more unverified copies for longer multiplies the hypothesis rather than testing it.

stem: An organisation wants to validate its incident response under realistic pressure, with responders using actual tooling against an injected scenario, without taking production down. Which exercise type fits?

options.text: A simulation
options.why: A simulation runs a realistic scenario with real tooling and real decisions, sitting between a discussion-based tabletop and an actual failover that moves production.

options.text: A tabletop exercise
options.why: A tabletop is discussion-based around a table. Nobody touches tooling, which is what the stem asks for.

options.text: A failover test
options.why: A failover test actually moves production to the secondary, which the stem rules out.

options.text: A penetration test
options.why: That assesses technical exploitability, not the response process.

stem: Which TWO statements about resilience design are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Redundant identical systems share every flaw those systems have, so diversity addresses a risk redundancy cannot
options.why: A common vulnerability across a fleet is a single point of failure however many instances exist.

options.text: Continuity of operations planning covers people and facilities, not only technology
options.why: The objectives split capacity planning across people, technology and infrastructure for exactly this reason.

options.text: A multi-cloud design removes the risk of customer misconfiguration
options.why: Your configuration errors replicate to every provider you deploy to.

options.text: Snapshots stored on the production array are an adequate substitute for offsite backups
options.why: They do not survive loss of the array, the site, or ransomware that can reach the storage.

options.text: Platform diversity reduces operational complexity
options.why: It increases it. More platforms means more expertise, patching and ways to misconfigure, which is the trade being made.
